items.title: Why He Hid 5,000 Jackscrews Under A Busy Hotel
items.description: In 1861, young engineer George Pullman placed 500 workers and 5,000 iron jackscrews beneath Chicago's six-story brick Tremont House hotel and hoisted the entire building six feet out of the swamp without closing for an hour. #shorts #history #engineering #fivestack

items.title: Why The Army Inflated Rubber Tanks In WWII
items.description: In 1944, the US Army Ghost Army deployed 93-pound inflatable rubber tanks and 500-pound truck speakers audible 15 miles away to trick German armies on D-Day. #shorts #history #ww2 #fivestack

items.title: Why The Navy Painted Warships Like Bright Zebras
items.description: In 1917, British marine artist Norman Wilkinson convinced Allied docks to paint over 4,000 warships in bright geometric Dazzle stripes to scramble German U-boat rangefinder optics by up to 40 degrees. #shorts #history #ww1 #fivestack

items.title: Why Cartographers Drew A Fake Town On Purpose
items.description: In the 1930s, General Drafting cartographers Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers invented a fake Catskills hamlet named Agloe from their scrambled initials to catch map copycats — until travelers saw Agloe on an Esso road map and built the real Agloe General Store there in 1950. #shorts #history #maps #fivestack

items.title: Why The Navy Built Cargo Ships Out Of Concrete
items.description: Facing a severe 1942 wartime steel plate shortage, the U.S. Maritime Commission ordered 24 steel-reinforced lightweight Haydite concrete cargo ships that floated via Archimedes' displacement and later served as permanent coastal breakwaters. #shorts #history #ww2 #engineering #fivestack

items.title: Why A Billionaire Mined Rocks With A Giant Claw
items.description: In 1974, billionaire Howard Hughes and the CIA disguised the massive 618-foot Hughes Glomar Explorer as a manganese nodule mining ship while secretly lowering a giant mechanical claw 16,500 feet to raise sunken Soviet submarine K-129. #shorts #history #coldwar #engineering #fivestack

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why Keyboard Letters Are Scrambled Out Of Order
topic_backlog.summary: Christopher Latham Sholes rearranged common adjacent letter pairs into QWERTY so neighboring mechanical typebars would stop colliding and jamming mid-word.

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why This Expensive London Townhouse Has Painted Windows
topic_backlog.summary: Numbers 23 and 24 Leinster Gardens in London look like grand five-story Victorian homes from the street until you see their 5-foot facade hiding open Metropolitan Line steam vents.

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why Engineers Mixed Sawdust Into Ship Ice
topic_backlog.summary: Project Habakkuk blended 14% wood pulp into water ice to create pykrete stronger than unarmored steel so a gunshot ricocheted off an ice block in front of admirals.

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why A Banker Mailed 40,000 Bricks Through The Post
topic_backlog.summary: William Coltharp shipped a bank's entire brick facade as parcel post crates across Utah mountains because 1916 USPS postage cost a fraction of wagon freight.

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why The Eiffel Tower Grows Six Inches Every Summer
topic_backlog.summary: Thermal expansion of 7,300 tons of puddled iron pushes the 330-meter tower upward by up to 15 cm and bends the sunward face away from Paris heat.

topic_backlog.title_idea: Why Engineers Curved Submarine Blades Like Banana Peels
topic_backlog.summary: Changing stiff symmetric bronze propeller blades to swept five- and seven-blade skewed geometry eliminated collapsing cavitation bubbles that gave submarines away on sonar.
